items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "food chain"?
options: An organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.
A network of interconnected food chains.
A diagram showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer.
An organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually using energy from sunlight through photosynthesis.
items.answer: A diagram showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer.
items.markingKey: Food chain: a diagram showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer.

items.stem: Explain why a food web is a more accurate description of feeding relationships than a food chain.
items.answer: Most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one type of organism; a web shows these interconnections.

items.stem: Explain why a pyramid of energy is never inverted.
items.answer: Energy is lost at each trophic level (respiration, heat, waste), so less is available to each level above.
items.markingKey: energy lost at each level [1]; less passed on [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia drew a food web for an African savanna: grass is eaten by zebras, gazelles and grasshoppers; acacia trees are eaten by giraffes and gazelles; grasshoppers are eaten by lizards and birds; lizards are eaten by birds; zebras are eaten by lions; gazelles are eaten by lions and cheetahs; giraffes are eaten by lions. (a) Write out the longest food chain in this web. (b) State the original source of energy for this food web.
items.answer: (a) grass → grasshoppers → lizards → birds (b) Sunlight (light energy captured by producers in photosynthesis).
items.markingKey: (a) grass → grasshoppers → lizards → birds [1] (b) [1]

items.stem: Amara drew a food web for a rice field: rice plants are eaten by grasshoppers, rats and planthoppers; weeds are eaten by grasshoppers; grasshoppers are eaten by frogs and spiders; planthoppers are eaten by spiders and frogs; spiders are eaten by frogs; frogs are eaten by snakes; rats are eaten by snakes and owls; snakes are eaten by owls. (a) Name one producer in this food web. (b) State the number of food chains in this food web. (c) Write out the longest food chain in this web.
items.answer: (a) rice plants (or weeds) (b) 8 (c) rice plants → grasshoppers → spiders → frogs → snakes → owls
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 8 [1] (c) rice plants → grasshoppers → spiders → frogs → snakes → owls [1]

items.stem: Noah drew a food web for a pond: algae are eaten by water fleas and pond snails; pondweed is eaten by pond snails and tadpoles; water fleas are eaten by dragonfly larvae and small fish; pond snails are eaten by small fish; tadpoles are eaten by dragonfly larvae and small fish; dragonfly larvae are eaten by small fish; small fish are eaten by herons. (a) State all the trophic levels at which the herons feed, and explain why. (b) Suggest the immediate effect on the population of small fish if all the herons were removed. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) 4, 5: they eat organisms at more than one level. (b) The population of small fish increases, because fewer are eaten (less predation).
items.markingKey: (a) all levels correct [1]; eats at more than one level [1] [2] (b) increases [1]; less predation [1] [2]

items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in a woodland. Arrows show who is eaten by whom: oak trees → caterpillars, aphids, deer; grass → rabbits, deer; caterpillars → blue tits, spiders; aphids → ladybirds, blue tits; ladybirds → blue tits; spiders → blue tits; blue tits → sparrowhawks; rabbits → foxes. (a) Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (b) Suggest why a food web is more stable than a single food chain.
items.answer: (a) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. (b) If one food source declines, consumers can eat other organisms, so populations are less affected.
items.markingKey: (a) energy lost at each level [1]; not enough for more levels [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in an African savanna. Arrows show who is eaten by whom: grass → zebras, gazelles, grasshoppers; acacia trees → giraffes, gazelles; grasshoppers → lizards, birds; lizards → birds; zebras → lions; gazelles → lions, cheetahs; giraffes → lions. (a) Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (b) Sketch and explain the shape of a pyramid of energy for the chain grass → grasshoppers → lizards.
items.answer: (a) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. (b) Each bar narrower than the one below; energy decreases at each level because of respiration, heat and waste.
items.markingKey: (a) energy lost at each level [1]; not enough for more levels [1] [2] (b) pyramid shape [1]; explanation [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "consumer"?
options: An organism that gets its energy from dead or waste organic material.
An organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.
An animal that gets its energy by eating plants.
An animal that gets its energy by eating other animals.
items.answer: An organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.
items.markingKey: Consumer: an organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.

items.stem: What do the arrows in a food chain represent?
items.answer: The direction of energy transfer
items.markingKey: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it.

items.stem: Explain why removing a species from a food web can affect organisms it does not eat.
items.answer: Its predators may eat more of other prey, and its prey increase and compete with other species; effects pass through the web.

items.stem: An ecologist in Santiago sampled a food chain: grass: number 472 750, mean dry mass 2.00 g; rabbits: number 71, mean dry mass 1500 g; stoats: number 55, mean dry mass 250 g. (a) Calculate the total dry biomass at each trophic level. (b) Calculate the biomass at the second trophic level as a percentage of that at the first. (c) Explain why biomass decreases at each trophic level.
items.answer: (a) grass 946 000 g; rabbits 107 000 g; stoats 13 800 g (b) 11.3% (c) energy (and biomass) is lost at each level by respiration, as heat, and in faeces and uneaten parts.
items.markingKey: (a) n × mass at each level [1]; all correct [1] (b) 107 000 ÷ 946 000 × 100 = 11.3% [1] (c) respiration / heat [1]; waste / uneaten parts [1] [5]

items.stem: Describe what is meant by a food chain and a food web, and compare pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy.
items.answer: Chain: energy transfer from producer to consumers; web: interconnected chains. Numbers: count organisms, may be inverted. Biomass: total dry mass, usually pyramid. Energy: energy per unit area per year, always pyramid.
items.markingKey: chain and web [2]; numbers [1]; biomass [1]; energy [1]; comparison / why shapes differ [1] [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the passing out of undigested food (faeces) from the body"?
items.answer: Egestion
items.markingKey: Egestion: the passing out of undigested food (faeces) from the body.

items.stem: Explain why energy flow through an ecosystem is described as non-cyclical.
items.answer: Energy enters as light and leaves as heat; it is not recycled, unlike nutrients such as carbon.

items.stem: Explain why warm-blooded animals (mammals, birds) have a lower efficiency of energy transfer than fish.
items.answer: They use much energy in respiration to keep a constant body temperature, and lose it as heat.

items.stem: In an ecosystem near Kathmandu, the energy in each trophic level was measured: algae 25 000 kJ/m²/year; water fleas 3 550 kJ/m²/year; small fish 359 kJ/m²/year. (a) Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from algae to water fleas. (b) Calculate the efficiency from water fleas to small fish. (c) Calculate the energy lost between algae and water fleas, and state two ways it is lost.
items.answer: (a) 14.2% (b) 10.1% (c) 21 450 kJ/m²/year; heat from respiration, faeces, uneaten parts, excretion.

items.stem: In an ecosystem near Mexico City, the energy in each trophic level was measured: rice 40 000 kJ/m²/year; rats 4 320 kJ/m²/year; snakes 626 kJ/m²/year. (a) Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from rice to rats. (b) Calculate the efficiency from rats to snakes. (c) Calculate the energy lost between rice and rats, and state two ways it is lost.
items.answer: (a) 10.8% (b) 14.5% (c) 35 680 kJ/m²/year; heat from respiration, faeces, uneaten parts, excretion.

items.stem: A hectare of farmland in Bogotá produces crops containing 2.0 × 10⁷ kJ of energy per year. One person needs about 3.5 × 10⁶ kJ per year. If the crops are fed to cattle, 10% of the energy is passed to beef. (a) Explain why the number of people fed is smaller when they eat beef. (b) Explain why keeping cattle indoors in warm sheds can increase the efficiency of energy transfer to beef.
items.answer: (a) An extra trophic level: cattle lose most energy in respiration (heat), faeces and urine, so only a small fraction becomes beef. (b) Less energy is used in movement and keeping warm, so more energy goes into growth (biomass).
items.markingKey: (a) extra trophic level [1]; energy lost by respiration / heat / waste [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why less energy is transferred to herbivores than to carnivores from their food.
items.answer: Plant material contains a lot of cellulose, which herbivores cannot digest fully, so more energy is lost in faeces.

items.stem: Sunlight falling on a field in Doha delivers 1.5 × 10⁶ kJ/m²/year. Crop plants capture 3% of this in photosynthesis. The efficiency of energy transfer between each later trophic level is 10%. (a) Calculate the energy in the producers. (b) Calculate the energy reaching the secondary consumers. (c) Suggest why only 3% of the light energy is captured by the plants.
items.answer: (a) 45 000 kJ/m²/year (b) 450 kJ/m²/year (c) light reflected, transmitted, wrong wavelength or misses chloroplasts; photosynthesis limited by CO₂ / temperature.

items.stem: Sunlight falling on a field in Dhaka delivers 1.5 × 10⁶ kJ/m²/year. Crop plants capture 1% of this in photosynthesis. The efficiency of energy transfer between each later trophic level is 10%. (a) Calculate the energy in the producers. (b) Calculate the energy reaching the secondary consumers. (c) Suggest why only 1% of the light energy is captured by the plants.
items.answer: (a) 15 000 kJ/m²/year (b) 150 kJ/m²/year (c) light reflected, transmitted, wrong wavelength or misses chloroplasts; photosynthesis limited by CO₂ / temperature.

items.stem: A hectare of farmland in Istanbul produces crops containing 3.6 × 10⁷ kJ of energy per year. One person needs about 3.0 × 10⁶ kJ per year. If the crops are fed to cattle, 10% of the energy is passed to beef. (a) Calculate how many people could be fed for a year by eating the crops directly. (b) Calculate how many people could be fed for a year by eating beef from cattle fed on the crops. (c) Explain why the number of people fed is smaller when they eat beef.
items.answer: (a) 12 people (b) 1.2 people (c) An extra trophic level: cattle lose most energy in respiration (heat), faeces and urine, so only a small fraction becomes beef.
items.markingKey: (a) 3.6 × 10⁷ ÷ 3.0 × 10⁶ [1] = 12 [1] [2] (b) 3.6 × 10⁷ × 0.1 = 3.6 × 10⁶ kJ [1]; ÷ 3.0 × 10⁶ = 1.2 [1] [2] (c) extra trophic level [1]; energy lost by respiration / heat / waste [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "bacteria that convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then nitrate ions"?
items.answer: Nitrifying bacteria
items.markingKey: Nitrifying bacteria: bacteria that convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then nitrate ions.

items.stem: Explain how the carbon in a dead tree is returned to the atmosphere.
items.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on the dead wood, digest it and respire, releasing carbon dioxide.
items.markingKey: decomposers [1]; respiration releases CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why farmers grow legumes such as beans in rotation with other crops.
items.answer: Root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria; when the plants are ploughed in, decomposition releases ammonium / nitrate, increasing soil fertility.

items.stem: Which process is described: ammonium ions are converted to nitrite and then nitrate ions by bacteria in the soil?
items.answer: Nitrification
items.markingKey: Ammonium ions are converted to nitrite and then nitrate ions by bacteria in the soil: nitrification.

items.stem: Name the process in which: (i) nitrogen gas is converted to ammonium or nitrate ions by bacteria (or by lightning); (ii) dead organisms are buried and compressed over millions of years, forming coal, oil and gas; (iii) carbon dioxide is taken in by green plants and converted to glucose.
items.answer: (i) nitrogen fixation (ii) fossilisation (iii) photosynthesis
items.markingKey: (i) nitrogen fixation [1] (ii) fossilisation [1] (iii) photosynthesis [1] [3]

items.stem: Name the process in which: (i) nitrogen gas is converted to ammonium or nitrate ions by bacteria (or by lightning); (ii) decomposers break down dead organisms, releasing carbon dioxide (and ammonium ions); (iii) dead organisms are buried and compressed over millions of years, forming coal, oil and gas.
items.answer: (i) nitrogen fixation (ii) decomposition (iii) fossilisation
items.markingKey: (i) nitrogen fixation [1] (ii) decomposition [1] (iii) fossilisation [1] [3]

items.stem: Ethan put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 0.5, 4.7, 19.3, 34.2, 29; trial 2: 0.3, 4.7, 18, 34.7, 30.5; trial 3: 0.5, 4.6, 18.1, 33.1, 29.1. (a) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Bags of leaves in sterilised (heated) soil — little decay should occur, showing that microorganisms cause the loss in mass. (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean percentage loss in mass on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and percentage loss in mass on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 0.7, 5.8, 22.1, 41.3, 52; trial 2: 0.7, 5.7, 22.3, 41.5, 37.2; trial 3: 0.7, 5.6, 23.4, 41.3, 35.4. (a) Explain the results. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) use enzymes; up to about 30–35 °C, more kinetic energy means faster enzyme activity and respiration, so faster decay; at higher temperatures the enzymes are denatured. (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean percentage loss in mass on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) decomposers / enzymes [1]; faster with more kinetic energy [1]; denaturation at high temperature [1] [3] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and percentage loss in mass on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the nitrogen in protein in a dead animal becomes nitrate in the soil.
items.answer: Decomposers break down protein to ammonium ions (ammonification); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrite then nitrate.
items.markingKey: decomposers / ammonium [1]; nitrifying bacteria [1]; nitrite → nitrate [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased over the last 200 years.
items.answer: Increased combustion of fossil fuels and deforestation (less photosynthesis, and burning releases CO₂).

items.stem: Tomás says: "Denitrifying bacteria add nitrate to the soil." Explain whether Tomás is correct.
items.answer: Denitrifying bacteria remove nitrate, converting it to nitrogen gas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Denitrifying bacteria remove nitrate, converting it to nitrogen gas. [2]

items.stem: Measurements at an observatory showed the mean carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere was 355 parts per million (ppm) in 1990 and 388 ppm in 2010. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase in ppm per year. (c) Suggest two human activities responsible for this increase.
items.answer: (a) 9.3% (b) 1.65 ppm per year (c) burning fossil fuels; deforestation.

items.stem: Mei put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 5.6, 24, 41.5, 37, 14.5; trial 2: 5.6, 22.4, 43.2, 38, 14.7; trial 3: 5.9, 23.5, 25.2, 38.3, 14.2. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (d) State the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: percentage loss in mass. (b) Trial 3 at 30 °C (25.2 %); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (c) Dry the leaves to constant mass before weighing. (d) They respire, releasing carbon dioxide from dead organic matter into the air.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = percentage loss in mass [1] [2] (b) trial 3 at 30 °C identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (c) Any one from: dry the leaves to constant mass before weighing; use several bags at each temperature; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a unit containing the community of organisms and their environment, interacting together"?
items.answer: Ecosystem
items.markingKey: Ecosystem: a unit containing the community of organisms and their environment, interacting together.

items.stem: Explain why a population of bacteria in a flask stops increasing after a time.
items.answer: Nutrients run out and toxic waste builds up (limiting factors), so the death rate rises to equal the birth rate.
items.markingKey: nutrients used up [1]; toxic waste [1]; death rate = birth rate [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the human population has grown so rapidly over the last 250 years.
items.answer: Better food supply, medicine, vaccination, sanitation and clean water reduced the death rate while birth rates stayed high.

items.stem: Aisha estimated the population of daisies on a school field in Jakarta measuring 20 m × 30 m. 10 quadrats, each 1 m², were placed at random. Number of daisies in each quadrat: 8, 11, 6, 10, 5, 15, 12, 9, 12, 12. (a) Suggest how the estimate could be made more reliable. (b) Suggest why counting daisies is easier with quadrats than counting animals such as beetles.
items.answer: (a) Use more quadrats (and calculate the mean). (b) Daisies do not move (or move very slowly), so they are not counted twice or missed.

items.stem: Omar estimated the population of dandelions on a school field in Cape Town measuring 20 m × 30 m. 10 quadrats, each 1 m², were placed at random. Number of dandelions in each quadrat: 20, 16, 18, 15, 17, 12, 12, 10, 18, 17. (a) Calculate the mean number of dandelions per quadrat. (b) Suggest why counting dandelions is easier with quadrats than counting animals such as beetles.
items.answer: (a) 15.5 (b) Dandelions do not move (or move very slowly), so they are not counted twice or missed.

items.stem: The world human population was about 2.5 billion in 1950 and about 8.0 billion in 2023. A demographer in Dubai predicts it will level off later this century. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in population. (b) Suggest two factors that could cause the population to level off.
items.answer: (a) 220% (b) Family planning / contraception lowering birth rate; limits of food, water and space; disease.

items.stem: In which phase of a sigmoid growth curve is the birth rate equal to the death rate?
items.answer: Stationary phase
items.markingKey: The population stays constant.

items.stem: A population of 100 bacteria doubles every 25 minutes in ideal conditions. How many will there be after 125 minutes?

A population of yeast cells was grown in a container in a laboratory in Lisbon. Time / hours: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Number (thousands per cm³): 8, 27, 83, 194, 309, 370, 391, 397. (a) Calculate the rate of increase in number between 6 and 8 hours. (b) Name the phase of growth between 10 and 14 hours and explain it. (c) Name the phase between 6 and 8 hours.
items.answer: (a) 57.5 per hour (b) stationary phase: limiting factors (food, space, waste) mean the birth rate equals the death rate (c) exponential (log) phase
items.markingKey: (a) (309 − 194) ÷ 2 [1] = 57.5 [1] (b) stationary [1]; limiting factor [1]; birth = death [1] (c) exponential [1] [6]

items.stem: A pyramid of numbers for oak tree → caterpillars → blue tits has a narrow base. Why?
options: One oak tree is very large and supports many caterpillars
items.answer: One oak tree is very large and supports many caterpillars
items.markingKey: Numbers do not account for size; biomass would give a normal pyramid.

items.stem: Explain why the pyramid of biomass for a sea can appear inverted when measured at one moment.
items.answer: Phytoplankton reproduce very quickly and are eaten rapidly, so their standing biomass is small even though their production is large.

items.stem: A student in Karachi states: "Arrows in a food chain show what eats what, pointing towards the food." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it, showing energy transfer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it, showing energy transfer. [2]

items.stem: Omar drew a food web for an African savanna: grass is eaten by zebras, gazelles and grasshoppers; acacia trees are eaten by giraffes and gazelles; grasshoppers are eaten by lizards and birds; lizards are eaten by birds; zebras are eaten by lions; gazelles are eaten by lions and cheetahs; giraffes are eaten by lions. (a) Name one producer in this food web. (b) Write out the longest food chain in this web.
items.answer: (a) grass (or acacia trees) (b) grass → grasshoppers → lizards → birds
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) grass → grasshoppers → lizards → birds [1]

items.stem: An ecologist in Muscat sampled a food chain: oak tree: number 1, mean dry mass 2 000 000 g; caterpillars: number 363 536, mean dry mass 0.800 g; blue tits: number 2 777, mean dry mass 11.0 g. (a) Calculate the total dry biomass at each trophic level. (b) Describe the shape of the pyramid of numbers. (c) Explain why the pyramid of biomass has a different shape from the pyramid of numbers.
items.answer: (a) oak tree 2 000 000 g; caterpillars 291 000 g; blue tits 30 500 g (b) narrow base (one or few large producers) with a wider second bar — not a true pyramid (c) biomass takes the mass of each organism into account; the producers are large, so the first trophic level has the greatest biomass and the biomass pyramid is a normal pyramid shape.
items.markingKey: (a) n × mass at each level [1]; all correct [1] (b) inverted / narrow base [1] (c) size taken into account [1]; producer biomass largest [1] [5]

items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in a rocky seashore. Arrows show who is eaten by whom: seaweed → limpets, periwinkles; phytoplankton → mussels, barnacles; limpets → crabs, gulls; periwinkles → crabs, dog whelks; mussels → dog whelks, gulls; barnacles → dog whelks; dog whelks → crabs; crabs → gulls. (a) Write out one food chain from this web with four organisms and label the trophic level of each. (b) Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (c) Explain the role of decomposers in this ecosystem.
items.answer: (a) seaweed (1) → periwinkles (2) → dog whelks (3) → crabs (4) (b) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. (c) They break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide and mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) for producers.
items.markingKey: (a) chain in correct order [1]; trophic levels [1] [2] (b) energy lost at each level [1]; not enough for more levels [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Approximately what percentage of energy is usually passed from one trophic level to the next?
items.markingKey: Typical efficiency is about 10% (range 5–20%).

items.stem: Explain why only a small percentage of the light energy falling on a field is captured by crop plants.
items.answer: Some light misses the leaves, is reflected, or is the wrong wavelength; photosynthesis is limited by other factors.

items.stem: A caterpillar eats plant material containing 2000 kJ of energy. 620 kJ is lost in faeces, 1000 kJ in respiration and 100 kJ in urine. (a) Calculate the energy used for growth (new biomass). (b) Calculate the percentage of the energy eaten that is used for growth. (c) Explain why so much energy is lost in the faeces of herbivores.
items.answer: (a) 280 kJ (b) 14% (c) plant cell walls contain cellulose, which is difficult to digest, so much remains undigested.

items.stem: Describe how energy flows through an ecosystem and explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient.
items.answer: Light → producers (photosynthesis, chemical energy) → consumers by feeding → decomposers; lost as heat. Losses: respiration (heat, movement), faeces, excretion, uneaten parts; ~10% passed on; limits chain length; eating lower in chain feeds more people.
items.markingKey: flow from Sun to producers to consumers [2]; three losses [3]; consequence (chain length / food production) [1] [6]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "nitrifying bacteria"?
options: Bacteria that convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then nitrate ions.
Bacteria that convert nitrate ions to nitrogen gas in anaerobic conditions.
A fuel such as coal, oil or natural gas formed from the remains of organisms over millions of years.
Swellings on the roots of legumes containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
items.answer: Bacteria that convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then nitrate ions.
items.markingKey: Nitrifying bacteria: bacteria that convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then nitrate ions.

items.stem: A student in Mexico City states: "Denitrifying bacteria add nitrate to the soil." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Denitrifying bacteria remove nitrate, converting it to nitrogen gas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Denitrifying bacteria remove nitrate, converting it to nitrogen gas. [2]

items.stem: Measurements at an observatory showed the mean carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere was 340 parts per million (ppm) in 1980 and 389 ppm in 2005. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase in ppm per year. (c) Suggest two human activities responsible for this increase.
items.answer: (a) 14.4% (b) 1.96 ppm per year (c) burning fossil fuels; deforestation.

items.stem: Nadia put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 0.6, 5.1, 19.6, 36.5, 31.1; trial 2: 0.6, 5.2, 20, 37.7, 31.3; trial 3: 0.6, 5, 20, 37.8, 33.2. State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean percentage loss in mass on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and percentage loss in mass on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 0.6, 4.8, 19.3, 35.6, 29.7; trial 2: 0.6, 2.8, 20, 35.9, 30.3; trial 3: 0.6, 4.9, 19.8, 37.1, 31. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: percentage loss in mass. (b) Dry the leaves to constant mass before weighing.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = percentage loss in mass [1] [2] (b) Any one from: dry the leaves to constant mass before weighing; use several bags at each temperature; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: A farmer in Muscat grows rice in a field that sometimes becomes waterlogged. In alternate years she grows clover (a legume) and ploughs it into the soil. (a) Explain why nitrate is lost from the soil when it is waterlogged. (b) Explain why the rice needs nitrate ions. (c) Describe how nitrate ions are absorbed by the roots.
items.answer: (a) Waterlogged soil is anaerobic; denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen gas. (b) To make amino acids and proteins for growth. (c) By active transport into root hair cells, using energy from respiration, against a concentration gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) anaerobic [1]; denitrifying bacteria [1] [2] (b) [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Explain the shape of the exponential (log) phase of a yeast growth curve.
items.answer: Plenty of food and space with little waste, so cells divide rapidly; birth rate much greater than death rate; numbers double at regular intervals.

items.stem: Explain why the death phase occurs in a closed culture of yeast.
items.answer: Food is used up and ethanol (toxic) accumulates, so the death rate exceeds the birth rate.

items.stem: A population of 200 yeast cells doubles every 90 minutes in ideal conditions. How many will there be after 360 minutes?
Describe and explain the shape of a sigmoid population growth curve for yeast grown in a flask of sugar solution.
items.answer: Lag: few cells, adapting, slow growth. Exponential: plenty of food, rapid division, numbers double regularly. Stationary: limiting factors (food, space, toxins); birth = death. Death: food used up, ethanol toxic, death > birth.
items.markingKey: lag [1]; exponential with reason [2]; stationary with reason [2]; death phase [1] [6]

items.stem: Which type of pyramid is always pyramid-shaped?
options: Pyramid of biomass measured on one day
items.answer: Pyramid of energy
items.markingKey: Energy is lost at each level, so each bar is smaller than the one below.

items.stem: Freya writes in a revision note: "Arrows in a food chain show what eats what, pointing towards the food." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it, showing energy transfer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it, showing energy transfer. [2]

items.stem: Tariq writes in a revision note: "A pyramid of biomass is the same as a pyramid of numbers." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: A pyramid of biomass shows the total dry mass at each level, which accounts for the size of organisms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: A pyramid of biomass shows the total dry mass at each level, which accounts for the size of organisms. [2]

items.stem: Amara drew a food web for a rice field: rice plants are eaten by grasshoppers, rats and planthoppers; weeds are eaten by grasshoppers; grasshoppers are eaten by frogs and spiders; planthoppers are eaten by spiders and frogs; spiders are eaten by frogs; frogs are eaten by snakes; rats are eaten by snakes and owls; snakes are eaten by owls. Suggest the immediate effect on the population of snakes if all the owls were removed. Explain your answer.
items.answer: The population of snakes increases, because fewer are eaten (less predation).
items.markingKey: increases [1]; less predation [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas drew a food web for a rice field: rice plants are eaten by grasshoppers, rats and planthoppers; weeds are eaten by grasshoppers; grasshoppers are eaten by frogs and spiders; planthoppers are eaten by spiders and frogs; spiders are eaten by frogs; frogs are eaten by snakes; rats are eaten by snakes and owls; snakes are eaten by owls. (a) Name one producer in this food web. (b) State the number of food chains in this food web. (c) Suggest the immediate effect on the population of snakes if all the owls were removed. Explain your answer. (d) State the original source of energy for this food web.
items.answer: (a) rice plants (or weeds) (b) 8 (c) The population of snakes increases, because fewer are eaten (less predation). (d) Sunlight (light energy captured by producers in photosynthesis).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 8 [1] (c) increases [1]; less predation [1] [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in a pond. Arrows show who is eaten by whom: algae → water fleas, pond snails; pondweed → pond snails, tadpoles; water fleas → dragonfly larvae, small fish; pond snails → small fish; tadpoles → dragonfly larvae, small fish; dragonfly larvae → small fish; small fish → herons. (a) Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (b) Explain the role of decomposers in this ecosystem. (c) Suggest why a food web is more stable than a single food chain.
items.answer: (a) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. (b) They break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide and mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) for producers. (c) If one food source declines, consumers can eat other organisms, so populations are less affected.
items.markingKey: (a) energy lost at each level [1]; not enough for more levels [1] [2] (b) [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which is not a way energy is lost between trophic levels?
options: Parts of the organism not eaten
items.answer: Photosynthesis
items.markingKey: Energy is lost by respiration (heat), excretion, egestion and uneaten parts.

items.stem: A student in Hanoi states: "Energy is recycled in an ecosystem like carbon." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Energy flows through the ecosystem and is lost as heat; only matter is recycled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Energy flows through the ecosystem and is lost as heat; only matter is recycled. [2]

items.stem: Sunlight falling on a field in Cape Town delivers 2.0 × 10⁶ kJ/m²/year. Crop plants capture 1% of this in photosynthesis. The efficiency of energy transfer between each later trophic level is 10%. (a) Calculate the energy in the producers. (b) Calculate the energy reaching the secondary consumers. (c) Suggest why only 1% of the light energy is captured by the plants.
items.answer: (a) 20 000 kJ/m²/year (b) 200 kJ/m²/year (c) light reflected, transmitted, wrong wavelength or misses chloroplasts; photosynthesis limited by CO₂ / temperature.

items.stem: A hectare of farmland in Mumbai produces crops containing 4.8 × 10⁷ kJ of energy per year. One person needs about 3.5 × 10⁶ kJ per year. If the crops are fed to cattle, 12% of the energy is passed to beef. (a) Calculate how many people could be fed for a year by eating the crops directly. (b) Explain why the number of people fed is smaller when they eat beef. (c) Explain why keeping cattle indoors in warm sheds can increase the efficiency of energy transfer to beef.
items.answer: (a) 13.7 people (b) An extra trophic level: cattle lose most energy in respiration (heat), faeces and urine, so only a small fraction becomes beef. (c) Less energy is used in movement and keeping warm, so more energy goes into growth (biomass).
items.markingKey: (a) 4.8 × 10⁷ ÷ 3.5 × 10⁶ [1] = 13.7 [1] [2] (b) extra trophic level [1]; energy lost by respiration / heat / waste [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Name the type of bacteria found in the root nodules of pea plants.
items.answer: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

items.stem: A student in Lagos states: "Plants get their nitrogen directly from the air through their leaves." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Plants absorb nitrate ions from the soil through root hair cells; most cannot use nitrogen gas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Plants absorb nitrate ions from the soil through root hair cells; most cannot use nitrogen gas. [2]

items.stem: Measurements at an observatory showed the mean carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere was 355 parts per million (ppm) in 1990 and 405 ppm in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase in ppm per year. (c) Suggest two human activities responsible for this increase.
items.answer: (a) 14.1% (b) 2 ppm per year (c) burning fossil fuels; deforestation.

items.stem: Arjun put 5.0 g of dried leaf discs in mesh bags with soil, kept them at different temperatures for 4 weeks, then dried and reweighed them to find the percentage loss in mass. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 4.9, 20.6, 37.7, 32.9, 12.8; trial 2: 4.9, 20, 36.7, 31.1, 13.2; trial 3: 5, 20.3, 36.7, 31.7, 12.7. State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean percentage loss in mass on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and percentage loss in mass on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Name the process in which: (i) excess amino acids are broken down in the liver, forming urea; (ii) nitrate ions are taken up by root hair cells by active transport; (iii) carbon compounds in plants pass to animals when they eat.
items.answer: (i) deamination (ii) absorption of nitrate (iii) feeding
items.markingKey: (i) deamination [1] (ii) absorption of nitrate [1] (iii) feeding [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe the carbon cycle and explain how human activities have changed the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
items.answer: Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decomposition and combustion return it; feeding passes carbon along food chains; fossilisation stores it. Humans burn fossil fuels and cut down forests, increasing CO₂.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis [1]; respiration / decomposition [1]; feeding [1]; fossilisation / combustion [1]; human activities [2] [6]

items.stem: Kwame estimated the population of plantains on a school field in Lisbon measuring 25 m × 60 m. 10 quadrats, each 0.5 m², were placed at random. Number of plantains in each quadrat: 5, 9, 8, 8, 9, 1, 9, 7, 5, 5. Suggest why counting plantains is easier with quadrats than counting animals such as beetles.
items.answer: Plantains do not move (or move very slowly), so they are not counted twice or missed.

items.stem: The world human population was about 1.6 billion in 1900 and about 8.0 billion in 2023. A demographer in Cairo predicts it will level off later this century. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in population. (b) Calculate the mean increase in billions per year. (c) Suggest two factors that could cause the population to level off.
items.answer: (a) 400% (b) 0.052 billion per year (c) Family planning / contraception lowering birth rate; limits of food, water and space; disease.
